details:
**Siege of Drogheda**
A 1649 siege during Cromwell's conquest of Ireland, after which his troops massacred the royalist garrison and many civilians and Catholic clergy. The commander Sir Arthur Aston was reportedly beaten to death with his own wooden leg, which soldiers believed held gold coins, and some survivors were shipped to Barbados. It remains the most notorious event of Cromwell's Irish campaign.

**Battle of Naseby**
The decisive 1645 battle of the First English Civil War, where the New Model Army under Sir Thomas Fairfax, with Cromwell commanding the cavalry, crushed Charles I's royalist army. Cromwell's son-in-law Henry Ireton was briefly captured there by Prince Rupert's cavalry.

**New Model Army**
The professional Parliamentarian (Roundhead) army created in 1645, first commanded by Sir Thomas Fairfax with Cromwell as his second-in-command and cavalry leader. Cromwell took overall command after Fairfax resigned in 1650, and the army became the base of his political power.

**Lord Protector**
The title Cromwell held from 1653 until his death in 1658 as head of state of the Commonwealth of England, Scotland, and Ireland. This period, between the execution of Charles I and the restoration of Charles II, is called the Interregnum or the Protectorate.

**Sir Thomas Fairfax**
The Parliamentarian general who commanded the New Model Army, with Cromwell serving under him at Marston Moor and Naseby. He resigned command in 1650 rather than invade Scotland, and Cromwell succeeded him.

**Execution of Charles I**
Cromwell signed the death warrant of King Charles I, who was beheaded in January 1649 for treason. After the Restoration, Cromwell's body was dug up and given a posthumous "execution" on the anniversary of Charles's death, alongside the bodies of the regicides John Bradshaw and Henry Ireton.

**Rump and Barebones Parliaments**
Pride's Purge in 1648 expelled moderate members from the Long Parliament, leaving the "Rump Parliament," which tried Charles I. In 1653 Cromwell dissolved the Rump, shouting "In the name of God, go!" and calling the Speaker's mace a "fool's bauble," and replaced it with the nominated Barebone's (Barebones) Parliament.

**Battle of Marston Moor**
A major 1644 Parliamentarian victory near York, where Cromwell's cavalry, nicknamed "Ironsides," helped defeat Prince Rupert of the Rhine. Cromwell's own nickname, "Old Ironsides," comes from Rupert.

**Siege of Wexford**
The second notorious massacre of Cromwell's 1649 Irish campaign, coming weeks after Drogheda. His troops broke into the town during surrender talks and killed the garrison, commanded by David Sinnott, and many civilians.

**Instrument of Government**
England's first written constitution, drafted in 1653 by General John Lambert, which made Cromwell Lord Protector. It was replaced in 1657 by the Humble Petition and Advice, which offered Cromwell the crown (he refused it) and let him name a new upper house and his successor.

**Putney Debates**
Debates in 1647 within the New Model Army on England's future constitution. Cromwell chaired them and, with Henry Ireton, opposed the radical Levellers and their manifesto An Agreement of the People, whose author John Lilburne he later imprisoned; Cromwell also put down Leveller mutinies.

**Richard "Tumbledown Dick" Cromwell**
Cromwell's son and successor as Lord Protector, who lacked support from the army and Parliament and resigned in 1659 after less than a year. His fall led to the restoration of Charles II in 1660.

**Battles of Dunbar and Worcester**
Cromwell beat the Scottish army of David Leslie at Dunbar on September 3, 1650, and won the final battle of the civil wars against Charles II at Worcester exactly one year later. At Worcester his troops used pontoon bridges to cross the rivers.

**Readmission of the Jews**
After the Whitehall Conference of 1655, held at the urging of the Dutch rabbi Manasseh ben Israel, Cromwell informally allowed Jews to live in England again. This reversed Edward I's Edict of Expulsion of 1290.

**Western Design**
Cromwell's 1654-1655 naval expedition against Spain's Caribbean colonies. It failed to take Hispaniola but captured Jamaica, and the Anglo-Spanish war also brought the Battle of the Dunes near Dunkirk.
